extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Tatler; literate coffeehouse/polite-society audience interested in manners, arts, literature, and politics (early 18th-century Britain)
extracted.subtask_description: Short periodical essay (The Tatler) offering commentary and criticism on social manners, theatre, poetry, painting, and current events, mixing news with judgments about taste and conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of female beauty and their effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarissa gains admiration; Chloe moves desire. Clarissa appears like a fine picture (artless, innocent of the torments she gives); Chloe strikes transport (conscious but not affected of her perfections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay contrasts two kinds of beauty and the different reactions they produce: Clarissa's beauty makes admirers melancholy and thoughtful, Chloe's makes them gay and well-pleased. The painter's representation (Jervas) should reflect these differences (Clarissa placed artless; Chloe drawn with liveliness). Examples: Clarissa as a shepherdess, Chloe as a country girl; Chloe's straw hat and riband represent a familiarity that 'cheats' the heart into feeling it has received a lover as well as an object of love. Effects on lovers are diagnostic: Chloe's love makes coxcombs; Clarissa's makes madmen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrait/painting should represent character by design
rubrics_metrics.description: A portrait's dress and pose must be imagined to represent the sitter's sort of beauty and its effect on observers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Jervas's design for Chloe (straw hat, riband) is praised for representing a beauty that 'enters the heart with a certain familiarity.' The painter's mastery is judged by how well clothing, pose, and expression convey the moral/psychological type of the sitter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theatre should engage the understanding, not merely senses
rubrics_metrics.description: The stage is 'an entertainment of the reason and all our faculties'; performances that please only the eyes and ears indicate a degeneracy of understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operas performed largely in Italian are criticized because 'the understanding has no part in the pleasure.' Mixing time/place/language/nation in a performance is condemned as confusing. The essay implies a standard: theatrical entertainments should involve and exercise reason and not merely provide shallow sensory gratification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and intelligibility matter in dramatic performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Performances that confuse languages or make large parts unintelligible fail to engage the audience's understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A critic is said to be so vexed by operas mixing languages that he will publish a treatise against them; the mixing of languages, places, and times is judged an 'incorrigible' confusion. This is an explicit criterion for evaluating opera and stagecraft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a good religious/political treatise
rubrics_metrics.description: The causes of an issue should be 'set forth in a clear and lively manner, without unseasonable passions'; language, sentiments, and reasonings should indicate the author's virtue and wisdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'Project for the Advancement of Religion' is praised because it treats the decay of religion with clarity and temperance; the author is judged credible because his style shows good breeding and balanced judgment. Good pamphleteering is measured by sober reasoning, absence of rant, and moral authority in tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate poetic diction and epithets
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic epithets must suit the actions and character in context; inappropriate or mechanical repetition is a fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic notes Homer's frequent epithets (e.g., 'nimble of foot' for Achilles) can be ludicrous when applied indiscriminately; Virgil is praised for selecting epithets (e.g., dropping 'pius' or 'pater' for 'dux Trojanus' in the Dido cave scene) that fit the circumstance. Criterion: diction must be congruent with the scene and character portrayed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholarly entertainment values new knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: At the Grecian Coffee-house, 'we think anything news which gives us new knowledge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Putting classics into a new light (e.g., a running 'journal' of the Iliad) is treated as a pleasant and valuable entertainment. The standard for what counts as news in this circle is novelty of insight or information, not merely current events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic love versus affectation in manners
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern pretenders to gallantry are accused of affectation and self-love; true devotion is distinguished from fashionable affectation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay laments that many in the age 'set up for wits' by repeating others' sayings, and that Cupid is 'dead-drunk' (i.e., love's faculties are impaired). Genuine love is exemplified by constancy and devotion (e.g., Cynthio's devotion), whereas ostentatious wit and vanity are signs of inauthentic passion. This offers evaluative criteria for judging conduct and sentiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pillars of greatness in public men
rubrics_metrics.description: Greatness (as in Marlborough) results from 'exact prudence, a calm courage, a well-governed temper, a patient ambition, and an affable behaviour.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political and military leaders are evaluated by these moral and temperamental qualities rather than by mere luck or single achievements. The essay uses Marlborough as exemplar: these arts are both the steps to greatness and its pillars once achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach of this miscellany: permissible novelty within bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: The author claims liberty to tell 'news' of things that escaped public notice or have been misrepresented, provided he stays 'within rules' and only errs in style and common speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This states an editorial standard for the periodical itself: it may reinterpret traditional stories or present overlooked facts to inspire admiration, but must not exceed the expected bounds of the Tatler in substance—informality of style is allowed, but not substantive impropriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public morality and the stage (anti-vice standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The theatre and public entertainments are to be criticized for promoting gaming, drunkenness, swearing, and immorality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Footnoted commentary (on Swift's 'Project') aligns with the Tatler's stance: stage entertainments should avoid encouraging vice, and a work defending religion is praised for attacking these corruptions. This supplies a moral standard for evaluating plays and theatrical culture.
